steps.explain: The board lights one of three steps. The phases where the core is getting its instruction (`FETCH`, and `WAIT_FETCH` while the bytes travel) light fetch.
`DECODE` lights decode: the core is working out what the 4 bytes mean.
`EXECUTE` lights execute, and so does `WAIT_DATA`: a `LOAD` or `STORE` is still doing its work, it's just waiting for memory's answer.
Every other phase (`IDLE`, `HALTED`, `FAULT`) means the core isn't running an instruction, so it shows as idle.

board-fetch-address.code:
const fetch = frame.packets.find((p) => p.type === "mem.read" && p.from === "cpu" && p.core === core && p.length === 4);
return fetch?.address ?? null;

steps.explain: A fetch is a `mem.read` the CPU sent for this core asking for 4 bytes: a whole instruction. A `LOAD` reads only 1 byte, so the length tells them apart.
The fetch's address is where this core's PC was. No fetch this tick: `null`, and the board shows nothing.
Work out what to draw: which step is lit, the three step names in order, the address being fetched (if any) and the title (core number, ⚡ in a handler, its program or idle).
With many cores each lane is short, so it's drawn on one row: the title on the left, and three small boxes on the right, the lit one in the core's colour.

Otherwise, the full card: the title at the top, three step boxes side by side (the lit one in the core's colour, with a thicker border), and the PC, the current instruction and any fetch address along the bottom.
Only replies matter here, and only replies to a request this CPU sent: look the request id (`replyTo`) up in `waiting` to find which core asked.
That request is answered now, so forget it.

Turn the bus message into the core's own kind of reply (`memData`, `memAck` or `memFault`) and hand it to that core. `receiveReply` keeps it for the next tick: the core only uses it then, like a flip-flop.
Each effect is a core asking memory for something. A read becomes a `mem.read` with the address and length, a write a `mem.write` with the bytes. `send` doesn't wait: it returns the new request's id.
Remember which core asked, under that id, so the reply can be handed to the right core when it comes back.
An instruction is 4 bytes. If they don't all fit before the end of memory, there's nothing valid to fetch: the core faults.
Otherwise the core doesn't call memory itself: it moves to `WAIT_FETCH` and returns a read effect for the 4 bytes at PC. The CPU shell sends it on the bus.
No reply yet: stay in `WAIT_FETCH` and count a stall. The core tries again next tick.
Memory said no (a fault), or sent something that isn't instruction bytes: the core can't go on, so it faults.
The bytes arrived: put them in the instruction register (IR) and move on to `DECODE`.
IR must hold exactly 4 bytes; anything else is a broken fetch.
Turn the 4 bytes into an instruction with your week-4 `decode`. A bad opcode, register or address faults, with where it happened.
A good instruction: keep it and move on to `EXECUTE`.
`LOAD` needs a byte from memory: return a 1-byte read effect and wait in `WAIT_DATA`. The register only changes when the byte arrives.

`ADD` adds two registers. A register holds 8 bits, so the result wraps (`& 0xff`). `zero` says the result is 0; `carry` says the real sum didn't fit. `finish` moves the PC on by 4 and goes back to `FETCH`.
`HALT` stops the core for good.
`STORE` returns a write effect with the register's byte and waits in `WAIT_DATA` for memory's ack.
`SUB` is like `ADD`: the result wraps to 8 bits, `zero` is set when it's 0, and `carry` means it went below 0 (a borrow).
`LOADI` puts the number from the instruction straight into the register: no memory trip. It sets `zero` and leaves `carry` as it was.
`JMP` always jumps: the PC becomes the address instead of moving on by 4.
`JZ` jumps when the last result was zero, `JNZ` when it wasn't. Not jumping is just the next instruction (PC + 4).
No reply yet: stay in `WAIT_DATA` and count a stall. A fault from memory faults the core.
A `LOAD` waits for `mem.data`: the byte goes in the register, `zero` follows it, and the core moves on (PC + 4, back to `FETCH`).
A `STORE` waits for `mem.ack`: memory wrote it, so the core moves on.
Any other reply means something went wrong: fault, and say what came instead.
The queue is the list in order, so the next program is simply the first one that's `READY`.
Find the program running on this core. If there isn't one, there's nothing to save: just clear the core.

Save it: its new state (`READY`, `DONE` or `FAILED`, checked by the process FSM), its context (registers, PC, flags) copied from the core, no core, and the instructions it ran there added to its count.
Move it to the back of the queue so the others get their turn, and clear the core for the next program.
